newsitem.title: UK: Britain faces water curbs as drought continues.
newsitem.headline: Britain faces water curbs as drought continues.

text.p: Britain, long seen as an island of grey skies and rain, is in the grip of its worst drought for 230 years and the summer is widely expected to see fresh curbs on use of water.
London, infamous for its fogs a century ago, has been drier than Istanbul or Madrid since last June, according to data from the British Meteorological Office.
Pleasure cruises along the River Thames west of London have had to be cancelled as the river slips to levels normally seen in August after a hot summer.
And while Britons basked in sunshine and record March temperatures over the Easter holiday last weekend, water companies are worrying.
Most vulnerable are those firms which supply England's south and east, historically the driest parts of the country and with denser population than the wetter north and west.
"It is a worrying situation. If there's no rain...well, we are not magicians," a spokesman for Thames Water, the company which supplies London, said on Wednesday.
Anglian Water, which covers eastern England, has seen rainfall drop from an average of 24 inches (61 centimetres) a year to 18 inches a year in the period since April 1995, a spokeswoman said.
"The situation is more challenging than it has been for some time," she said.
Anglian reckoned in February that it would need an inch of rain a week during April to bring supplies back to a "comfortable" level, "that's way more than we can expect," the spokeswoman said.
Thames Water would need at least average rainfall over the next few months to avoid having to introduce bans in an area which has not had restrictions on the use of hosepipes in gardens since 1990.

Companies are keen to avoid a re-run of 1995 when the hottest summer on record triggered bans across the country on non-essential water use and Yorkshire Water, in northern England, was nearly forced to curb essential domestic supplies.
Yorkshire was fined by industry regulator Ofwat for its poor performance and has subsequently changed management and invested in new systems which should avoid similar problems.
"We are not complacent but we are confident that we will be able to go through the summer without any restrictions to customers," a company spokesman said.

Water companies have spent over 500 million pounds ($824.4 million) since 1995 investing in systems aimed at securing supplies and cutting leakage, which was running at over 800 million gallons a day last year and triggered sharp criticism from the opposition Labour party and consumer groups.
But companies are also hoping that they can persuade customers themselves to contribute by curbing the amount of water used.
A garden hose running for an hour uses the same amount of water as an average family of four would require in a day, for example.

Thames Water has produced leaflets with London's world-famous Kew Gardens showing customers that gardens only need watering once a week and companies have issued users with information on how to cut down other domestic use.
Metering is also a popular method of encouraging customers to trim their use with some companies now offering free installations.
"We have to make the best use of the water that we do have," said a spokesman for Southern Water.
Southern still has a ban on the use of hosepipes for Sussex, south of London, which it introduced last summer and has not ruled out further restrictions, he added.
But even if customers curb demand and the companies maintain supplies this summer, there are concerns that the problems may not be over.

"Dealing with this sort of rainfall situation may become the norm...I think we've started to base our longer-term proposals on the basis that we are undergoing dramatic (climate) change," the Southern spokesman said.
($ = 0.606 British Pounds)
